newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy law would allow exiled king's son to return.
newsitem.headline: Italy law would allow exiled king's son to return.

text.p: The Italian cabinet on Friday drafted a law to allow the son of the last king to return from a 50-year exile but said the move was not an attempt to dismiss the past.
If the bill is passed, Vittorio Emanuele, 59, will be allowed home for the first time since he was forced into exile with his father, King Umberto II, as a nine-year-old.
The cabinet said in a statement that the draft bill, which must be passed by both houses of parliament before it can become law, was not an attempt to rewrite history.
"The law does not represent...any revision of ethical and political judgements on events which are consigned to history," the statement said.

Italians threw out their monarchy in 1946 in favour of a republic, blaming them for complicity with more than 20 years of fascist rule under dictator Benito Mussolini, who led Italy into World War Two on the Nazi side.
The law worked out on Friday proposes to lift the post-war republic's decision to ban the last king Umberto II and the male line of his family from ever returning to Italy.
Umberto II took his family to Portugal and then Switzerland, where he died in 1983, leaving Vittorio Emanuele as his heir.
He has said he will not renounce his royal prerogatives but the new bill said members of the House of Savoy would be barred from political activity and from voting in the Italian republic.

Economic weekly magazine Il Mondo said in an article to be published on Saturday that the Savoy dynasty still had around one trillion lire ($600 million) in wealth, some in the form of property confiscated by the republic soon after their exile.
The magazine said the royal family had 800 billion lire in assets invested in the United States and a further 104 billion in interest payments on a life insurance policy pay-out.
It said the family could also stake a claim for the return of confiscated property, including two castles, the Savoy villa and even the crown jewels if they contested ownership in court.
Vittorio Emanuele caused outrage last week when he refused to apologise for fascist anti-semitic laws passed in 1938 when his grandfather, Vittorio Emanuele III, was head of state.
The leader of Rome's Jews, Rabbi Elio Toaff, called the laws, which threw Jews out of schools and jobs, a "disgrace which cannot be erased from the history of the House of Savoy".

The hard-left Communist Refoundation party, whose support gives Prime Minister Roman Prodi a parliamentary majority, said earlier this week it was opposed to the return of Vittorio Emanuele in the light of his comments.
"It is an unheard-of disgrace that he did not say sorry to Italians for the racial laws and for taking Italy into war," Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said. ($1=1,670)
